results.title: Complementary literal
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The complement of a literal $(x, b)$ with variable $x$ and polarity $b$ is the literal $(x, \lnot b)$: the same variable with the opposite polarity.

results.title: Tseitin clauses for a conjunction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For literals $g$, $a$ and $b$, the defining clauses of the gate literal $g$ for the conjunction of $a$ and $b$ are, in this order, the three clauses $\lnot g \lor a$, $\lnot g \lor b$ and $g \lor \lnot a \lor \lnot b$, where $\lnot \ell$ denotes the complementary literal of $\ell$ (same variable, opposite polarity).

results.title: Tseitin clauses for a disjunction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For literals $g$, $a$ and $b$, the defining clauses of the gate literal $g$ for the disjunction of $a$ and $b$ are the three clauses $\lnot g \lor a \lor b$, $g \lor \lnot a$ and $g \lor \lnot b$, where $\lnot \ell$ denotes the complementary literal of $\ell$.

results.title: Tseitin clauses for an implication
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For literals $g$, $a$ and $b$, the defining clauses of the gate literal $g$ for the implication from $a$ to $b$ are, in this order, the three clauses $\lnot g \lor \lnot a \lor b$, $g \lor a$ and $g \lor \lnot b$, where $\lnot \ell$ denotes the complementary literal of $\ell$ (same variable, opposite polarity).

results.title: One step of the Tseitin encoding
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a rule $\mathit{cl}$ assigning to literals $g$, $a$, $b$ a list of defining clauses, and the results $(a, C_A, k_A)$ and $(b, C_B, k_B)$ of encoding the two operands of a binary connective (each a literal, a clause list and a next unused gate number), the step returns the positive literal $g$ of variable $2k_B+1$, the clause list $C_A$, then $C_B$, then $\mathit{cl}(g, a, b)$, and the next gate number $k_B+1$.

results.title: One step of the linear-time Tseitin builder
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $c$ map a gate literal and two operand literals to a list of clauses, and let $(a, \varphi_A, k_A)$ and $(b, \varphi_B, k_B)$ be the results for the two operands, each a literal, a clause list and a next free gate number. The step returns the positive literal $g$ of the variable $2k_B + 1$, the clause list $c(g, a, b)$ followed by $\varphi_B$, and the next free gate number $k_B + 1$. Neither $\varphi_A$ nor…

results.title: Connective count of a propositional formula
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a propositional formula $A$, built from atoms with the binary connectives $\wedge$, $\vee$ and $\to$, the connective count of $A$ is the number of occurrences of these connectives in $A$. It is $0$ for an atom, and for $B \circ C$, with $\circ$ one of $\wedge$, $\vee$ and $\to$, it is the count of $B$ plus the count of $C$ plus $1$.

results.title: Tseitin encoding with gates numbered from $k$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Fix a map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers. Given a formula $A$ and a gate number $k$, the encoding returns a literal naming $A$, a list of defining clauses and the next unused gate number. For an atom $a$ it returns the positive literal of variable $2\iota(a)$, no clauses, and $k$. For $A \circ B$ with $\circ$ one of $\wedge$, $\vee$, $\to$, it encodes $A$ from gate $k$, obtaining a literal $a$, clauses $C_A$…

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Fix a map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers. Given a formula $A$, a gate number $k$ and a clause list $\mathit{acc}$, the builder returns a literal naming $A$, a clause list and the next unused gate number. For an atom $a$ it returns the positive literal of variable $2\iota(a)$, the list $\mathit{acc}$ unchanged, and $k$. For $A \circ B$ with $\circ$ one of $\wedge$, $\vee$, $\to$, it runs on $A$ from gate $k$…

results.title: The linear-time Tseitin builder agrees with the reference encoding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers, every formula $A$, every gate number $k$ and every clause list $\mathit{acc}$, the linear-time Tseitin builder run on $A$ from gate $k$ with accumulator $\mathit{acc}$ returns the same literal naming $A$ and the same next unused gate number as the reference Tseitin encoding of $A$ with gates numbered from $k$, and its clause list is $X$ followed by $\mathit{acc}$…

results.title: Tseitin CNF
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers and a formula $A$, run the linear-time Tseitin builder on $A$ with gates numbered from $0$ and the empty accumulator, obtaining a literal $\ell$ naming $A$ and a clause list $C$. The Tseitin CNF of $A$ is the unit clause $[\ell]$ followed by $C$.

results.title: The Tseitin CNF reorders the reference encoding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers and every formula $A$, the Tseitin CNF of $A$ is the unit clause whose literal is the literal naming $A$ in the reference Tseitin encoding of $A$ with gates numbered from $0$, followed by a list of clauses that is a permutation of the defining clauses of that encoding.

results.title: Tseitin CNF with $\bot$ false
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an atom type with a distinguished atom $\bot$, a map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers and a formula $A$, this is the CNF consisting of the unit clause whose literal is the negative literal of variable $2\iota(\bot)$, followed by the Tseitin CNF of $A$ with respect to $\iota$.

results.title: Number of defining clauses in the Tseitin encoding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers, every formula $A$ and every gate number $k$, the list of defining clauses produced by the Tseitin encoding of $A$ with gates numbered from $k$ has length $3c$, where $c$ is the number of binary connectives of $A$.

results.title: Number of clauses of the Tseitin CNF
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every proposition $A$ and every map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers, the Tseitin CNF of $A$ with respect to $\iota$, as a list of clauses counted with repetition, has length $3c + 1$, where $c$ is the number of binary connectives of $A$: three defining clauses per connective plus the unit clause asserting $A$.

results.title: Tseitin clauses have at most three literals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every proposition $A$ and every map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers, every clause of the Tseitin CNF of $A$ with respect to $\iota$ has at most three literals.

results.title: Truth value of a literal
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ assign a Boolean value to every natural-number variable, and let $\ell = (x, b)$ be a literal with variable $x$ and polarity $b$. The truth value of $\ell$ under $\sigma$ is true exactly when $\sigma(x) = b$.

results.title: Satisfying a concatenation of CNF formulas
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every assignment $\sigma$ of Boolean values to the natural-number variables and all CNF formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$, $\sigma$ satisfies the formula consisting of the clauses of $\varphi$ followed by those of $\psi$ if and only if $\sigma$ satisfies both $\varphi$ and $\psi$.

results.title: Gate variables in a range
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $k'$, a variable $x \in \mathbb{N}$ is a gate in range $[k, k')$ if $x = 2j + 1$ for some $j \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le j < k'$.

results.title: Allowed variables for a gate range
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $k'$, a variable $x \in \mathbb{N}$ is allowed for the gate range $[k, k')$ if $x$ is even (it names an atom) or $x$ is a gate in range $[k, k')$, that is, $x = 2j + 1$ for some $j \in \mathbb{N}$ with $k \le j < k'$.

results.title: Functions of the atom variables
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A function $f$ from assignments $\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Bool}$ to Booleans depends only on the atom variables if $f(\sigma) = f(\tau)$ for all assignments $\sigma$ and $\tau$ with $\sigma(2n) = \tau(2n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

results.title: Tseitin encoding invariant
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $k$ be a natural number, let $r = (\ell, \Phi, k')$ consist of a literal $\ell$, a CNF formula $\Phi$ and a natural number $k'$, and let $v$ map each assignment of Boolean values to the natural-number variables to a Boolean value. Call a variable a gate in range if it equals $2j + 1$ for some $j$ with $k \le j < k'$. The invariant holds for $k$, $r$ and $v$ when $k \le k'$; the variable of $\ell$ and every…

results.title: Satisfaction depends only on the occurring variables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula and let $\sigma$ and $\tau$ be assignments of Boolean values to the natural-number variables that agree on every variable occurring in a literal of $\varphi$. If $\sigma$ satisfies $\varphi$, then $\tau$ satisfies $\varphi$.

results.title: Value of a proposition read off the atom variables
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Given a map $\iota$ from atoms to natural numbers, a proposition $A$ and an assignment $\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Bool}$, this is the truth value of $A$ under the valuation that gives each atom $a$ the value $\sigma(2\iota(a))$.

results.title: Correctness invariant of the Tseitin encoding
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\iota$ map atoms to natural numbers, let $A$ be a proposition and $k$ a natural number, and let $(\ell, \Phi, k')$ be the reference Tseitin encoding of $A$ with gates numbered from $k$: the literal naming $A$, its defining clauses and the next unused gate number. For an assignment $\sigma$ of Boolean values to the natural-number variables, let $A[\sigma]$ be the truth value of $A$ when each atom $a$ gets the…

results.title: Tseitin correctness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\iota$ be an injective map from atoms to natural numbers, let $A$ be a proposition and let $v$ be a valuation of the atoms. Then $A$ is true under $v$ if and only if some assignment $\sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathrm{Bool}$ with $\sigma(2\iota(a)) = v(a)$ for every atom $a$ satisfies the Tseitin CNF of $A$ with respect to $\iota$.

results.title: Equisatisfiability of the Tseitin transformation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the atoms have a distinguished atom $\bot$, let $\iota$ be an injective map from atoms to natural numbers and let $A$ be a proposition. The Tseitin CNF of $A$ with respect to $\iota$, together with the unit clause making the variable $2\iota(\bot)$ false, is satisfiable if and only if $A$ is true under some valuation $v$ of the atoms with $v(\bot)$ false.

Let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$, and let $(b_i^*)_{i \in \iota}$ be its dual basis of…

results.title: Evaluation of the dual basis
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $M$ and $N$ be $A$-modules, let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect pairing, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$. Write $(b_i^\vee)_{i \in \iota}$ for the dual basis of $b$ with respect to $B$, a basis of $M$. Then for all $i, j \in \iota$, the value $B(b_i^\vee, b_j)$ equals $1$ if $j = i$ and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Uniqueness of the dual basis
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $M$ and $N$ be $A$-modules, let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect pairing, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$. If $b' = (b'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is a basis of $M$ such that for all $i, j \in \iota$ the value $B(b'_i, b_j)$ equals $1$ if $j = i$ and $0$ otherwise, then $b'$ is the dual basis of $b$ with respect to $B$.

results.title: Existence of a dual basis for a perfect pairing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $M$ and $N$ be $A$-modules, let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect pairing, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$. Then there is a basis $(b'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of $M$ such that for all $i, j \in \iota$ the value $B(b'_i, b_j)$ equals $1$ if $j = i$ and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Existence and uniqueness of the dual basis for a perfect pairing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, let $M$ and $N$ be $A$-modules, let $B : M \times N \to A$ be a perfect pairing, and let $b = (b_i)_{i \in \iota}$ be a basis of $N$ indexed by a finite type $\iota$. Then there is exactly one basis $(b'_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of $M$ such that for all $i, j \in \iota$ the value $B(b'_i, b_j)$ equals $1$ if $j = i$ and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: MC-finite sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An integer sequence $s$ is MC-finite if for every natural number $m > 0$ it eventually satisfies, modulo $m$, a linear recurrence with constant integer coefficients: there are natural numbers $p > 0$ and $q > 0$ and integers $c_0, \dots, c_{p-1}$ such that $s(n + p) \equiv \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} c_i\, s(n + i) \pmod{m}$ for all $n \ge q$.

results.title: Polynomial recursions give MC-finite sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $u_0, \dots, u_k$ be integer sequences and let $P_0, \dots, P_k$ be polynomials with integer coefficients in $k + 2$ variables such that $u_i(n+1) = P_i(u_0(n), \dots, u_k(n), n)$ for every $i \le k$ and every $n \ge 0$. Then the sequence $u_0$ is MC-finite.

results.title: P-recursive sequences with leading coefficient 1 are MC-finite
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be an integer sequence that is P-recursive of order $k$ with coefficient polynomials $Q_0, \dots, Q_k$ with integer coefficients, that is, $Q_0(n)\, s_n = \sum_{i=1}^{k} Q_i(n)\, s_{n-i}$ for every $n \ge k$. If $Q_0 = 1$, then $s$ is MC-finite.

results.title: Polynomially recursive integer sequences are MC-finite
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Call an integer sequence $s$ MC-finite if for every natural number $m > 0$ there are natural numbers $p > 0$ and $q > 0$ and integers $c_0, \dots, c_{p-1}$ such that $m$ divides $s(n + p) - \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} c_i\, s(n + i)$ for all $n \ge q$. Every integer sequence $s$ has the following two properties.

results.title: Smolensky: parity is not in AC0(mod 3)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The parity language, which accepts a bitstring exactly when an odd number of its entries are true, is not in $\mathsf{AC}^0[3]$, the class $\mathsf{AC}^0[m]$ for $m = 3$ of decision problems decided by polynomial-size, bounded-depth families of well-formed flat Boolean circuits in which every mod gate has modulus $3$.

results.title: Order-statistic tree node entry
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A node entry of an order-statistic tree over a type $\alpha$ consists of a key in $\alpha$ and a natural number, the cached number of nodes in the subtree rooted at that node.

results.title: Order-statistic tree
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An order-statistic tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is a binary tree, possibly empty, each of whose nodes carries a key in $\alpha$ together with a natural number, meant as the cached number of nodes in the subtree rooted at that node. That these caches are correct is a separate condition.

results.title: Cached root size
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The cached root size of an order-statistic tree is the subtree size stored in the entry of its root node, and is $0$ for the empty tree.

results.title: Erasing the size caches of an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The erasure of an order-statistic tree is the binary tree of the same shape whose node keys are the keys of the original nodes: the empty tree is sent to the empty tree, and a node is sent to the node with the same key whose left and right subtrees are the erasures of the original left and right subtrees, so every cached subtree size is dropped.

results.title: Correct size caches
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An order-statistic tree has correct size caches when, at every node, the cached subtree size equals the number of nodes of the left subtree plus the number of nodes of the right subtree plus one, that is, the number of nodes of the subtree rooted at that node. The empty tree has correct size caches.

results.title: Ordered order-statistic tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An order-statistic tree over a type equipped with a relation $<$ is ordered when the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached sizes is an ordered binary search tree: at every node, each key of the left subtree is $<$ the node's key, the node's key is $<$ each key of the right subtree, and both subtrees are ordered.

results.title: Inorder traversal of an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The inorder traversal of an order-statistic tree is the inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached subtree sizes: the traversal of the left subtree, then the root key, then the traversal of the right subtree, and the empty list for the empty tree.

results.title: Order-statistic tree node with computed cache
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a key $k$ and order-statistic trees $L$ and $R$, the node built from them has key $k$, left subtree $L$, right subtree $R$, and cached subtree size equal to the cached root size of $L$ plus the cached root size of $R$ plus one, where the empty tree has cached root size zero.

results.title: Search in an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $q \in \alpha$. Searching for $q$ in the empty tree returns false. At a node with key $k$, the search continues in the left subtree if $q < k$, continues in the right subtree if $k < q$, and returns true otherwise.

results.title: Insertion into an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Inserting a key $k$ of a linearly ordered type into the empty tree gives a single node with key $k$ and cached size $1$. For a nonempty tree with root key $r$: if $k < r$, the key is inserted into the left subtree; if $r < k$, it is inserted into the right subtree; in both cases the root is rebuilt with key $r$ and cached size equal to the cached root sizes of its two subtrees plus one (an empty subtree counts as…

results.title: Order-statistic tree built from a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, the order-statistic tree built from a list of keys is obtained by inserting the keys into the empty tree from right to left: the empty list gives the empty tree, and a list with head $k$ and tail $l$ gives the insertion of $k$ into the tree built from $l$.

results.title: Rank in an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $q$ of a linearly ordered type, the rank of $q$ in an order-statistic tree is computed by descending from the root. It is $0$ for the empty tree. At a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, it is the rank of $q$ in $L$ if $q < k$; it is $s(L) + 1$ plus the rank of $q$ in $R$ if $k < q$; and it is $s(L)$ if $q = k$. Here $s(L)$ is the subtree size cached at the root of $L$, and $0$ if…

results.title: Select in an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an order-statistic tree $T$ and a natural number $i$, select at index $i$ in $T$ is computed by descending from the root. It returns nothing for the empty tree. At a node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, it is select at index $i$ in $L$ if $i < s(L)$; it returns $k$ if $i = s(L)$; and it is select at index $i - s(L) - 1$ in $R$ if $i > s(L)$. results.title: Correct caches give the tree size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an order-statistic tree $T$ has correct cached subtree sizes at every node, then the cached root size of $T$ (zero for the empty tree) equals the number of nodes of $T$.

results.title: The cache-computing node constructor preserves correct size caches
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $k$ be a key and let $L$ and $R$ be order-statistic trees whose cached subtree sizes are correct at every node. Then the node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, whose root cache is the cached root size of $L$ plus the cached root size of $R$ plus one, also has correct cached subtree sizes at every node.

results.title: Insertion commutes with forgetting the size caches
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$. Forgetting the cached sizes of the tree obtained by inserting $k$ into $T$ gives the same binary tree as inserting $k$, by ordinary binary-search-tree insertion, into $T$ with its cached sizes forgotten.

results.title: Insertion preserves correct size caches
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $k \in \alpha$, and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ whose cached subtree sizes are correct at every node. Then the tree obtained by inserting $k$ into $T$ also has correct cached subtree sizes at every node.

results.title: Insertion preserves ordering of order-statistic trees
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered key type that is ordered, meaning that after its cached sizes are erased, at every node each key of the left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's key and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger. Then for every key $k$, the tree obtained by inserting $k$ into $T$ is again ordered.

results.title: Order-statistic trees built from a list have correct size caches
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $\ell$ of elements of $\alpha$, the order-statistic tree obtained by inserting the elements of $\ell$ into the empty tree, from right to left, has correct cached subtree sizes at every node.

results.title: Order-statistic trees built from lists are ordered
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $l$ of keys from a linearly ordered type, the order-statistic tree built from $l$ by successive insertion is ordered: after its cached sizes are erased, at every node each key of the left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's key and each key of the right subtree is strictly larger.

results.title: Keys of an order-statistic tree built from a list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, a key $k$ and a list $l$ of keys, $k$ is a key of some node of the order-statistic tree built from $l$ by successive insertion if and only if $k$ occurs in $l$.

results.title: Search in an ordered order-statistic tree is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered: after forgetting the cached sizes, at every node all keys in the left subtree are smaller than the node's key and all keys in the right subtree are larger. Then for every $q \in \alpha$, comparison search for $q$ in $T$ returns true if and only if $q$ is the key of some node of $T$.

results.title: Cached rank agrees with traversal rank
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered key type whose cached subtree sizes are correct at every node and which is ordered. Then for every query $q$, the rank of $q$ computed by descending $T$ with cached left-subtree sizes equals the number of entries strictly smaller than $q$ in the inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained by erasing the caches of $T$.

results.title: Cached select agrees with inorder select
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every order-statistic tree $T$ whose cached subtree sizes are correct and every natural number $i$, select at index $i$ in $T$ (descending with the cached sizes) returns the same result as taking the element at zero-based position $i$ of the inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached sizes; in particular both return nothing when that position does not exist.

results.title: Select inverts rank in an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered type whose cached subtree sizes are correct and which satisfies the binary-search-tree ordering. For every key $k$ in $T$, select in $T$ at the index equal to the rank of $k$ in $T$ returns $k$.

results.title: Rank inverts select in an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered type whose cached subtree sizes are correct and which satisfies the binary-search-tree ordering. If select at zero-based index $i$ in $T$ returns a key $k$, then the rank of $k$ in $T$ equals $i$.

results.title: Merging order-statistic trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The merge of order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$ is defined by recursion on $A$. If $A$ is empty, it is $B$. If $A$ has root key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$, it is the node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree the merge of $R$ and $B$, whose cached size is the sum of the cached root sizes of its children plus one, an empty child counting as zero. Thus $B$ is attached below the rightmost…

results.title: Deletion from an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Deleting a key $k$ from an order-statistic tree over a linearly ordered type follows the comparison path from the root. The empty tree stays empty. At a node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$: if $k < x$, the result is the node with key $x$, left subtree the deletion of $k$ from $L$ and right subtree $R$; if $x < k$, it is the node with key $x$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree the deletion of…

results.title: Order-statistic merge preserves cache correctness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ and $B$ be order-statistic trees whose cached subtree size at every node equals the number of nodes in that node's subtree. Then the merge of $A$ and $B$ has the same property. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is assumed.

results.title: Order-statistic deletion preserves cache correctness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ a key and $T$ an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$. If the cached subtree size at every node of $T$ equals the number of nodes in that node's subtree, then the same holds for the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$.

results.title: Merging separated ordered order-statistic trees preserves order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $L$ and $R$ be ordered order-statistic trees over $\alpha$ such that $x < y$ for every key $x$ of $L$ and every key $y$ of $R$. Then the merge of $L$ and $R$ is ordered.

results.title: Deletion preserves order in an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, after its cached sizes are removed, every key in a left subtree is strictly smaller than the key of its node and every key in a right subtree is strictly larger. Then for every key $k$, the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$ is again ordered.

results.title: Inorder traversal of an order-statistic merge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$, the inorder traversal of the merge of $A$ and $B$ is the inorder traversal of $A$ followed by the inorder traversal of $B$. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is assumed.

results.title: Keys of an order-statistic merge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For order-statistic trees $A$ and $B$ over a type $\alpha$ and any $x \in \alpha$, $x$ is a key of the merge of $A$ and $B$ if and only if $x$ is a key of $A$ or a key of $B$. No ordering between the keys of $A$ and $B$ is assumed.

results.title: Inorder traversal after order-statistic deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key). The inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ is the inorder traversal of $T$ with every occurrence of $k$ removed.

results.title: Keys of an order-statistic tree after deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key). For every $y \in \alpha$, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ if and only if $y$ is a key of $T$ and $y \ne k$.

results.title: Deleted key is absent from an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key). Then $k$ is not a key of the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$.

results.title: Search misses a key deleted from an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $k \in \alpha$ and $T$ an ordered order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ (at every node, all keys of the left subtree are smaller and all keys of the right subtree are larger than the node's key). Comparison search for $k$ in the tree obtained by deleting $k$ from $T$ returns false.

results.title: Rank after deletion in an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered and whose cached subtree sizes are correct. Let $k$ and $q$ be keys and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$. Then the rank of $q$ in $T'$, computed by navigation with cached sizes, equals the number of entries strictly smaller than $q$ in the inorder traversal of $T'$ with its cached sizes…

results.title: Selection after deletion in an order-statistic tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ whose cached subtree sizes are correct. Let $k$ be a key and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$. Then for every natural number $i$, selecting position $i$ in $T'$ by navigation with cached sizes returns the entry at zero-based position $i$ of the inorder traversal of $T'$ with its cached sizes removed,…

results.title: Selecting the rank of a surviving key after deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $T$ be an order-statistic tree over $\alpha$ that is ordered and whose cached subtree sizes are correct, let $k$ be a key, and let $T'$ be the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $k$. If $y$ is a key of $T'$, then selecting, with cached sizes, the position in $T'$ given by the cached rank of $y$ in $T'$ returns $y$.

results.title: Access cost
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The cost of accessing an item $x$ in a list $L$ is its position in $L$, counting from $1$: one more than the index of the first occurrence of $x$ in $L$. If $x$ does not occur in $L$, the cost is the length of $L$ plus one.

results.title: Move-to-front
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $L$ and an item $x$, moving $x$ to the front gives the list consisting of $x$ followed by $L$ with its first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur in $L$, this is $x$ followed by $L$.

results.title: Cost of move-to-front
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Starting from a list $L$, move-to-front serves a request sequence $\sigma$ one request at a time: a request $x$ costs the position of $x$ in the current list, counting from $1$ (an item not in the list costs its length plus one), and then $x$ is moved to the front (inserted at the front if absent). The cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ from $L$ is the sum of these access costs.

results.title: Final list of move-to-front
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Starting from a list $L$ and serving a request sequence $\sigma$, move-to-front moves each request $x$ in turn to the front of the current list (inserting it at the front if it is absent). The final list of move-to-front on $\sigma$ from $L$ is the list it ends with.

results.title: Inversion set of two lists
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For lists $M$ and $L$, the inversion set is the set of pairs $(a, b)$ of items of $M$ with $a$ before $b$ in $M$ and $b$ before $a$ in $L$, that is, the pairs that $M$ and $L$ order differently. Here the position of an item in a list is the index of its first occurrence, and an item that does not occur in the list sits at the position equal to the length of the list.

results.title: Number of inversions between two lists
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For lists $M$ and $L$, the number of inversions of $L$ against $M$ is the size of their inversion set: the number of pairs $(a, b)$ of items of $M$ with $a$ before $b$ in $M$ and $b$ before $a$ in $L$, where the position of an item in a list is the index of its first occurrence, or the length of the list if it does not occur.

results.title: Offline cost without free exchanges
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, the offline cost of a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost of $x_t$ in $L_t$ (its position, counting from $1$) plus the number of inversions between $L_t$ and $L_{t+1}$. That is, the algorithm serves request $t$ with $L_t$ and then rearranges it into $L_{t+1}$, paying one for each pair of items whose relative order it…

results.title: Free move
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A free exchange (Sleator and Tarjan): right after accessing $x$ in a list $L$, move $x$ forward to index $j$ (indices counted from $0$), at no charge. If the index of $x$ in $L$ is at most $j$, the list is unchanged, so $x$ never moves backward for free; otherwise the result is obtained by erasing the first occurrence of $x$ from $L$ and inserting $x$ back so that it has index $j$.

results.title: Offline cost with free exchanges
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given lists $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$, target indices $J_0, J_1, J_2, \dots$ and a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$, let $L_t'$ be the list obtained from $L_t$ by the free exchange that moves $x_t$ forward to index $J_t$ (counting from $0$); it equals $L_t$ if $x_t$ already has index at most $J_t$. The offline cost with free exchanges of $\sigma$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost of $x_t$ in…

results.title: Indices after erasing an entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a list with no repeated entries and let $a \ne x$ be entries of $M$. After erasing $x$ from $M$, the index of $a$ is unchanged if $a$ comes before $x$ in $M$, and is one less if $a$ comes after $x$ (indices counted from $0$).

results.title: Move-to-front keeps the relative order of the other items
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a list without duplicates, $x$ an item of $M$, and let $M'$ be the list obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the front. For any items $a \ne x$ and $b \ne x$ of $M$, $a$ comes before $b$ in $M'$ if and only if $a$ comes before $b$ in $M$.

results.title: Counting the entries before an entry
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ is a list with no repeated entries and $x$ is an entry of $L$, then the number of entries of $L$ whose index is less than the index of $x$ equals the index of $x$ (indices counted from $0$).

results.title: Members of the inversion set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ and $L$ be lists. If a pair $(a, b)$ belongs to the inversion set of $M$ and $L$, then $a$ and $b$ are items of $M$, $a$ comes before $b$ in $M$, and $b$ comes before $a$ in $L$. Here the position of an item in a list is the index of its first occurrence, and an item that does not occur in the list sits at the position equal to the length of the list.

results.title: Triangle inequality for inversions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$, $L$ and $L'$ be lists with $L$ a rearrangement of $M$. Then the number of inversions of $L'$ against $M$ is at most the number of inversions of $L$ against $M$ plus the number of inversions of $L'$ against $L$.

Let $\Phi$ be the number of inversions between $M$ and $L$ (the pairs of items that the two lists order differently), and $\Phi'$ the number of inversions between the list obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the front and $L$. results.title: Move-to-front rearranges the list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $x$ is an item of a list $M$, then the list obtained from $M$ by moving $x$ to the front is a rearrangement (permutation) of $M$.

results.title: A free move rearranges the list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $x$ is an item of a list $L$, then for every index $j$ (counting from $0$), the list obtained from $L$ by the free move of $x$ to index $j$ is a rearrangement (permutation) of $L$.

results.title: Free moves never add inversions against a list headed by the moved item
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list without duplicates, $x$ an item of $L$, and $N$ a list that is empty or starts with $x$, all of whose items occur in $L$. For every $j \in \mathbb{N}$, let $L'$ be the list obtained from $L$ by moving $x$ forward for free so that exactly $j$ items precede it, where $L' = L$ if at most $j$ items already precede $x$ in $L$. Then the number of inversions of $L'$ against $N$ is at most the number of…

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a list without duplicates, $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$, $L_0, L_1, \dots$ lists that are each a rearrangement of $M$, and $J_0, J_1, \dots$ natural numbers. Accessing the item at position $i$ of a list, counting from $1$, costs $i$. results.title: Without free moves the two offline costs agree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a natural number and let $L_0, L_1, L_2, \dots$ be lists, each of length at most $K$. Take every free-exchange target to be $K$; this moves nothing, since every item already has index at most $K$. Then for every request sequence $\sigma$, the offline cost with free exchanges of serving $\sigma$ with $L_0, L_1, \dots$ equals the offline cost without free exchanges of serving $\sigma$ with $L_0, L_1, \dots$.

results.title: Amortized bound for move-to-front over a request sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a list without duplicates, $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$, and $L_0, L_1, \dots$ lists that are each a rearrangement of $M$. Accessing the item at position $i$ of a list, counting from $1$, costs $i$. Let $C$ be the total access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$, $F$ the list it ends with, and $D$ the cost on $\sigma$ of the offline algorithm without free…

Consider an offline algorithm given by lists $L_0, L_1, \ldots$, each a rearrangement of $M$ with $L_0 = M$, and natural numbers $J_0, J_1, \ldots$. results.caption: Theorem

Consider an offline algorithm that serves request $t$ with a list $L_t$, where every $L_t$ is a rearrangement of $M$ and $L_0 = M$: it pays the position of the request in $L_t$ (counting from $1$), and then one for each pair of items whose relative order differs between $L_t$ and $L_{t+1}$. results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a list of distinct items, $L$ a rearrangement of $M$, and $\sigma$ a sequence of $m$ requests, each an item of $M$. Then the access cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from $M$, plus $m$, is at most twice the cost of serving $\sigma$ with the fixed list $L$ (the sum over the requests of their positions in $L$, counting from $1$), plus the number of inversions between $M$ and $L$ (the pairs of…

results.title: Deterministic online list-update algorithm
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of `M`: a state machine whose list is always a rearrangement of `M`. Its rearrangements are free, which only strengthens the lower bound.

results.title: Cost of an online list-update algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The cost of a deterministic online list-update algorithm $A$ on a request sequence $x_1, \dots, x_m$ from a state $q_0$ is $c_1 + \dots + c_m$, where $q_i$ is the state $A$ moves to from $q_{i-1}$ on request $x_i$ and $c_i$ is the access cost of $x_i$ in the list of state $q_{i-1}$. The empty sequence costs $0$.

results.title: The list-update adversary
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a deterministic online list-update algorithm $A$, a default item $d$, a number $n$ and a state $q$ of $A$, the adversary's sequence is the sequence of $n$ requests that starts in state $q$, always requests the last item of $A$'s current list, and then moves $A$ to its next state on that request. If the current list is empty, the default item $d$ is requested instead.

results.title: The list of an algorithm on a nonempty list is never empty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of a nonempty list $M$. Then in every state of $A$, the list of $A$ is nonempty.

results.title: The adversary makes every access cost the full length of the list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a nonempty list of $\ell$ distinct items and let $A$ be a deterministic online list-update algorithm on the items of $M$. For every default item $d$, every natural number $n$ and every state $q$ of $A$, the cost of $A$ from state $q$ on the adversary's sequence of $n$ requests from $q$ with default item $d$ is $n \ell$.

results.title: Online move-to-front
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $M$, online move-to-front is the online list-update algorithm on the items of $M$ whose states are the rearrangements of $M$, starting from $M$ itself: on a request $x$ that is in the current list it moves $x$ to the front, and it ignores requests that are not in the current list.

results.title: Online move-to-front pays the move-to-front cost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a list and $\sigma$ a request sequence whose requests are all items of $M$. From any state of online move-to-front on $M$, its access cost on $\sigma$ equals the cost of move-to-front on $\sigma$ starting from the list of that state.

results.title: Static cost
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The static cost of serving a request sequence $\sigma = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{m-1}$ with a fixed list $L$ is the sum over $t < m$ of the access cost of $x_t$ in $L$, its position in $L$ counting from $1$.

results.title: The static cost is the offline cost of a constant list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ and every request sequence $\sigma$, the offline cost (without free exchanges) of serving $\sigma$ with the constant sequence of lists $L, L, L, \dots$ equals the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with $L$.

results.title: Positions in a list and in its reverse
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ is a list of length $\ell$ with no repeated entries and $x$ is an entry of $L$, then the access cost of $x$ in $L$ plus the access cost of $x$ in the reverse of $L$ equals $\ell + 1$: the positions of $x$ in $L$ and in its reverse, counting from $1$, add up to $\ell + 1$.

results.title: A list or its reverse serves any sequence at average cost at most $(\ell + 1)/2$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a list of $\ell$ distinct items. For every request sequence $\sigma$ of $m$ items of $L$, the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with $L$ plus the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with the reverse of $L$ equals $m(\ell + 1)$.

results.title: Inversions are at most the squared length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any lists $M$ and $L$, the number of inversions of $L$ against $M$ is at most $\ell^2$, where $\ell$ is the length of $M$.

results.title: Switching lists after the first request
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a list of length $\ell$ and $R$ a list, and write $\mathrm{inv}(M, R)$ for the number of inversions between $M$ and $R$. For every request sequence $\sigma$ of items of $M$, the offline cost (without free exchanges) of serving $\sigma$ with the lists $M, R, R, R, \dots$ is at most $\ell + \mathrm{inv}(M, R)$ plus the static cost of serving $\sigma$ with $R$.
